When design meets code: navigating both worlds

There's a conversation that happens in tech — often, annoyingly — that goes like this: are you a designer or a developer?

I used to stumble on that question. Now I answer it differently: yes.

The hyphen as a home

In typography, a hyphen connects. It creates compound words — things that couldn't exist as either half alone. That's what I think about when people ask me to choose a side.

I'm a front-end developer. I write JavaScript, wrangle CSS specificity, argue with myself about whether to use a div or a section. But I also care deeply — obsessively — about whether the spacing feels right. Whether the color contrast passes WCAG. Whether the component hierarchy mirrors the visual hierarchy.

These aren't separate skills. They're the same skill, viewed from different angles.

What designers taught me about code

The best thing I ever did for my code was study design:

Constraints are generative. A 4px grid, a limited type scale, a set color palette — constraints don't limit creativity, they direct it. The same is true in code. Good architecture is a set of constraints that makes the right thing easy and the wrong thing hard.

Names matter enormously. A designer who can't name a component hasn't finished thinking about it. A developer who names their variables data and thing and temp hasn't finished thinking either. Naming is design.

The user is not you. This sounds obvious. It is not obvious when you're deep inside a codebase, solving what feels like a purely technical problem. Someone will interact with this. That person deserves your attention.

What code taught me about design

And the reverse is true:

Everything is a system. Once you've built a design system in code, you can never look at a design file the same way. Inconsistencies become visible. Patterns reveal themselves. You start asking: is this a component, or a variant? Should this be a token?

Details compound. A 1px misalignment in code becomes invisible at small scale and glaring at large scale. Designers know this. Developers learn it, usually painfully, in production.

Iteration is survival. You don't ship the perfect component. You ship the component, observe what happens, and refactor. Design works the same way — or at least, it should.

Where I'm going

I want to build things that work and things that feel right. I want to write code that a designer would understand and design interfaces that a developer could build without screaming.

That hyphen is where I live. I'm learning to love it there.
